title: The Toddy Tapper's Sudden Shaking — Alcohol, Hypoglycemia, and a Night of Involuntary Movements

sections.heading: The Patient's Story
sections.content:
He is 75 years old and taps toddy for a living. Eight years before this admission, a fall from giddiness led to a diagnosis of low blood pressure; an X-ray at the time raised the possibility of a right hip fracture, but he never had it treated. Two years ago he was diagnosed with COPD. He has smoked hand-rolled cigarettes for 40 years and has been drinking 90–180 mL of alcohol daily for the same span.

The day before admission, he became unresponsive and was taken to a local hospital, where his blood glucose was found critically low, at 22 mg/dL, and was treated. He seemed to recover and was normal through the night — until, at 1 a.m., he suddenly developed involuntary movements of his right arm and leg. His attenders reported his last drink had been three days earlier. There was no rolling up of the eyes, tongue-biting, incontinence, or facial deviation reported, but shortness of breath began abruptly around the same time, severe enough to limit him significantly.

sections.heading: What the Work-Up Showed So Far
sections.content:
- General exam: no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or pedal edema
- Vitals: temperature 99.7°F, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse 125 bpm, respiratory rate 38/min, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, capillary glucose 97 mg/dL
- Neurological exam: Glasgow Coma Scale E1V1M5 (eyes and verbal responses absent, withdrawing to pain); cranial nerves could not be assessed; tone normal in the upper limbs and right leg, increased in the left leg; reflexes symmetric and normal; plantar responses flexor bilaterally; sensory and cerebellar exam could not be assessed due to his level of consciousness; no neck rigidity or meningeal signs
- Respiratory exam: diffuse wheeze on both sides, with dullness to percussion at the right lower chest
- Investigations sent: arterial blood gas, complete blood picture, urine examination, fasting lipid profile, renal and liver function tests, thyroid profile, chest X-ray, ECG, ultrasound abdomen, 2D echocardiogram, and MRI brain

sections.heading: How the Story Unfolded on the Ward
sections.content:
His working diagnosis was an acute exacerbation of COPD with left upper lobe fibrosis, alongside new-onset seizures thought secondary to alcohol withdrawal. He was started on intravenous fluids, an anti-seizure medication (levetiracetam), hydrocortisone, thiamine and a B-complex injection, nebulization with a steroid and mucolytic followed by chest physiotherapy, and nasogastric feeding with milk and protein powder, alongside regular glucose and vital sign monitoring.

By the next day his involuntary movements had decreased and he regained consciousness, though his Glasgow Coma Scale remained reduced (E4V1M6). His antibiotics were escalated to ceftriaxone, and chlordiazepoxide (Librium) was started for alcohol withdrawal, alongside continued thiamine, anti-seizure medication, hydrocortisone, and nebulization. Over the next several days he continued to improve — becoming conscious and coherent, tolerating oral intake, with his Glasgow Coma Scale rising to E4V5M6 — while diffuse wheeze on both sides persisted and his working diagnosis remained the same. He was discharged at his own request after four days, still on his withdrawal and COPD regimen.
